lesson_title: The Ash That Weighs More Than the Fuel
hook_text: Burn a strip of magnesium and the white powder left behind is heavier than the metal you started with. Fire did not make mass. So where did it come from?
clip_script: Hold a strip of magnesium in a flame. It burns with a light so white you have to look away. Left behind: a white powder. Weigh it, and it is heavier than the ribbon. Fire did not create anything. The magnesium grabbed oxygen atoms out of the air, and those atoms have mass: magnesium plus oxygen gives magnesium oxide. And the recipe never changes. Three grams of magnesium always take exactly two grams of oxygen and make five grams of product. Give it extra and the extra is just left over. Compounds can be taken apart too. Heat green copper carbonate: it turns black and breathes out carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. Run electricity through water: hydrogen bubbles at one rod, oxygen at the other, always twice as much hydrogen, because water is H2O. A burning splint makes the hydrogen pop. Atoms are never made or destroyed. They just change partners.
visual_style: A whiteboard balance with a magnesium ribbon on one side, then the heavier white powder tipping it; then two upturned test tubes over water, one with twice the gas of the other, labelled H2 and O2.
pacing: A question at the start, a quick explanation, a fast pair of decomposition demos, and a crisp final rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and calculate how much product any recipe makes.
